subtype: Approach: preparing specific questions in advance [Thinking]
passage:
Monday night. Mahima worked through the probability sheet and stopped at question six. In the margin went a note: "I don't see why these events are independent. My attempt gives 0.4, which looks wrong." Mahima thought, if I bring my working, they can see where I'm stuck instead of guessing. Three unclear points went on a list, stapled to the attempt.

Wednesday, office hours. Mahima put the pages on the professor's desk. "I tried this and it breaks here." The professor read for a minute and said the trouble was only in how the sample space had been set up. Ten minutes were enough.

Friday. Farida asked how it went. "Better than I feared. They knew exactly where to look."

qa.q: What did Mahima staple to the list of unclear points?
qa.a: Mahima stapled the attempt to the list of three unclear points.

qa.q: What was Mahima thinking while writing the margin note on Monday night?
qa.a: Mahima reasoned that bringing the working would let the professor see where the confusion was, so no one would need to guess.

qa.q: What other approach could Mahima use if the office hour is full, and why?
qa.a: Mahima could send the list and the attempt by email first, because the professor could read them before replying.

qa.q: How might the professor see a student who arrives with an attempt and a list?
qa.a: The professor can find the confusion in minutes and use the time well, since the student has already shown the exact step where it breaks.

grounding: A student writes down what is unclear, tries the problem first and brings the work so the professor can locate the confusion quickly.

subtype: Approach: choosing office hours and a polite email [Action]
passage: In Jatin's small college town, the professor came in from the city only three days a week, and the local bus was the one way back. Jatin sat on the shop step and typed an email on the phone: "Respected Sir or Madam, I am a second-year student. Could I have fifteen minutes during your office hours on Thursday? I want to ask about the derivations in the fourth chapter." Nitin, waiting for the same bus, read over the shoulder and said the subject line was too plain. Jatin changed it to the chapter number and the word "doubts". On Thursday the notes were in a folder, and the whole talk fit inside the fifteen minutes.

qa.q: How many minutes did Jatin ask for in the email?
qa.a: Jatin asked for fifteen minutes during the office hours on Thursday.

qa.q: What might Jatin have been feeling about taking up the professor's time?
qa.a: Jatin seems careful and a little nervous about asking, so the polite email with a clear topic shows respect for the professor's limited days.

qa.q: What could Jatin try if there is no reply by Wednesday?
qa.a: Jatin could send one short reminder and mention the same topic, because the professor is only in town a few days a week and may have missed the first message.

qa.q: How might Nitin see Jatin's changes to the subject line?
qa.a: Nitin probably sees a clearer request that the professor can understand at a glance and answer more quickly.

grounding: A student in a small town emails for a short office-hours slot, names the topic and brings notes, respecting the professor's time.

subtype: Approach: avoiding asking out of fear of looking foolish [Pitfall]
passage:
Outside the exam hall Mridul held up the result sheet. "Binita, you lost marks on the whole probability section. You told me in September that it made no sense."

"I know."

"Then why didn't you ask the professor?"

"They would have thought I was weak. Everyone else seemed to follow. I kept telling myself I would work it out before the test."

"And now?"

Binita looked at the floor. "Now I have to go to the retest and I still don't understand the first chapter. I spent months worrying instead of asking, and it only got bigger." Mridul folded the sheet. "One question in September would have saved all that."

qa.q: What did Binita say the professor would have thought?
qa.a: Binita said the professor would have thought Binita was weak.

qa.q: What was Binita worried about when staying silent for months?
qa.a: Binita feared looking weak in front of the professor and the others, and hoped to work it out alone before the test.

qa.q: What could Binita try before the retest, and why would it help?
qa.a: Binita could bring a short list of the parts that make no sense to the professor, because a clear question shows effort and gets a direct answer.

qa.q: How might Mridul see Binita's silence?
qa.a: Mridul seems worried and a little frustrated, having watched a friend lose marks that one question might have saved.

grounding: A student stays silent for fear of looking foolish, the confusion grows until the exam and marks fall.

subtype: Approach: mentally rehearsing the first sentence [Thinking]
passage:
Dear Disha,

You asked how I finally spoke to the professor, so here is the secret. Two nights before, I couldn't sleep, so I practised one sentence in the mirror: "I tried the second question and got stuck at the step where I change the variable." I said it in the corridor, on the stairs, and under my breath at the tea stall. I thought, if I know the first line, the rest will follow. And it did. My voice shook for a moment, but then the professor asked to see the step and we were away. It was about six minutes.

Try it before your viva. It really helps! 🙂

Tenzin

qa.q: What sentence did Tenzin practise in the mirror?
qa.a: Tenzin practised: I tried the second question and got stuck at the step where I change the variable.

qa.q: What did Tenzin think would happen once the first line was ready?
qa.a: Tenzin believed that once the opening line was ready the rest of the talk would follow, and that turned out to be right.

qa.q: What else could Disha do to feel ready for the viva, and why?
qa.a: Disha could write the likely first question and say the opening aloud with a friend, since practice makes the first words feel familiar.

qa.q: How might the professor see Tenzin's opening sentence?
qa.a: The professor sees exactly what was tried and where it broke, so the professor can start helping at once. 🙂

grounding: A nervous student practises a specific opening line and finds it much easier to begin the conversation.

subtype: Approach: vague requests that get vague answers [Pitfall]
passage: After the Friday lecture on signals, Yamini waited at the front of the lecture room until the others left. "Professor, I didn't understand anything today." The professor asked which part. "All of it, honestly. I feel lost." So the professor turned to the board and went through the first ten minutes of the lecture again, slowly, with the same examples. Yamini nodded at each step and said "okay" but kept looking at the clock. Afreen, waiting at the door for a lift home, saw the professor sigh quietly and Yamini leave with the same blank look. Neither had got what they hoped for. In the corridor Yamini muttered, "That did not help at all."

qa.q: What did Yamini say to the professor at the front of the room?
qa.a: Yamini said, Professor, I didn't understand anything today.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling while nodding and looking at the clock?
qa.a: Yamini felt lost and frustrated, since repeating the whole lecture did not touch the actual confusion.

qa.q: What could Yamini say next time to get a better answer, and why?
qa.a: Yamini could name the one step or example that stopped making sense, because a precise question lets the professor explain exactly that part.

qa.q: How might the professor feel when the only request is that nothing made sense?
qa.a: The professor may feel stuck and a little frustrated, since there is no clue where the trouble is and repeating the lecture is the only option.

grounding: A student says only that nothing was understood, the professor can only repeat the lecture, and both are frustrated.

subtype: Approach: asking for guidance on a project or recommendation [Action]
passage: At a university in a small Dutch town, Mei wanted a professor who had taught a good seminar to guide a research project on river pollution. Mei wrote a one-page outline first, with the question, a rough method and two sources. Kofi read it over coffee and said to cut the second aim, so it was tighter. Then Mei knocked on the office door. "Could you look at this outline and tell me what you think? I am not asking you to supervise yet, only for feedback." The professor read for a while, said the method was solid but the scope was wide, and suggested one paper to read before next month. Mei wrote it down and said thank you.

qa.q: What did Mei put in the one-page outline?
qa.a: The outline had the question, a rough method and two sources.

qa.q: What did Mei want from the professor, and why did Mei avoid asking for supervision yet?
qa.a: Mei wanted honest advice without pressing for a promise, and hoped to make the request easy for the professor to answer.

qa.q: What could Mei try next, and why?
qa.a: Mei could revise the outline using the advice and send it back with a short thanks, because it shows the feedback was used and may lead to further help.

qa.q: How might the professor see a student who arrives with a short outline?
qa.a: The professor can respond to something concrete in a short time, and is not pushed into a commitment.

grounding: A student asks a professor who taught well for project advice, brings a short outline and asks for feedback rather than a promise.

subtype: Approach: requesting an extension with honesty and a plan [Action]
passage: Tuesday, 9 p.m. I was away for four days because of a family emergency and the term paper is due Friday. Sarita told me at lunch to write to the professor today, not on the last day. So I did. I said I had been away, said I would need until the following Wednesday, and attached a scan of the travel tickets. I did not make it sound worse than it was. I just wrote what happened and when I would submit. The reply came within the hour: "Thank you for telling me early. Wednesday is fine." I am so relieved I could cry. I still have work to do, but at least it has a date now. Sangeeta

qa.q: What did Sangeeta attach to the email?
qa.a: Sangeeta attached a scan of the travel tickets.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when the professor's reply came?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt very relieved, so much that the diary says it could bring tears.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do next to make sure the new date is kept, and why?
qa.a: Sangeeta could set small daily targets for the paper, since a date is only helpful if the work is split into steps.

qa.q: How might the professor see an early, honest request with a date?
qa.a: The professor can trust the reason and plan around it, since Sangeeta wrote early and gave a clear date without exaggerating.

grounding: After a family emergency a student tells the professor early, proposes a date with proof and does not exaggerate, and receives a fair answer.

subtype: Approach: using a peer or teaching assistant first [Thinking]
passage: The test was in three days and the professor's only office hour was Friday, after it. Vishal stared at the notes on eigenvalues and asked, half aloud, "Which of these can Manjula help with?" Two doubts were about basic method: how to set up the matrix and where the signs go. Manjula, a final-year senior, had done the course last year. The third was different: why a certain result holds at all. "That one needs someone who really knows the theory," Vishal said. "I will not waste the professor's time on the signs." So the two basic doubts went to Manjula that evening, and the conceptual one was written on a slip to email to the professor before Friday.

qa.q: How many days were left before the test?
qa.a: There were three days left before the test.

qa.q: What did Vishal think about which doubt suited Manjula and which suited the professor?
qa.a: Vishal was thinking that basic method could be handled by a senior and the deeper conceptual question was better saved for the professor.

qa.q: What could Vishal do if Manjula cannot explain the signs either?
qa.a: Vishal could try a classmate or look at a worked example, because a basic doubt often has a quick answer somewhere before the professor.

qa.q: How might Manjula see being asked the basic doubts?
qa.a: Manjula probably feels useful and glad to help, since the course was finished last year and these are doubts a senior can answer.

grounding: A student takes basic doubts to a senior and saves conceptual ones for the professor, matching the helper to the problem, under time pressure.

subtype: Approach: following up with a thank-you and progress [Revision]
passage: My name is Noor, and for two years I only went to my professor when I was drowning. I would ask, get an answer, mumble thanks and vanish. Then the professor said at the end of one meeting, "Let me know how it goes." I noticed that I never had. So this time I fixed the errors and the next day sent a short message: "Thank you for Tuesday. Your tip about the boundary condition fixed the whole second section." Two weeks later I brought a new draft and a fresh question. The professor remembered the earlier one. I had always thought asking for help was a single favour. It turned out to be the start of a conversation.

qa.q: What did Noor's professor say at the end of the meeting?
qa.a: The professor said, Let me know how it goes.

qa.q: What did Noor realise after the professor's remark?
qa.a: Noor noticed that Noor had never reported back after getting help, and understood that a thank-you with progress was missing.

qa.q: What else could Noor do to keep the relationship going, and why?
qa.a: Noor could share a short note whenever a paper or project reaches a milestone, because small updates show the professor's time had an effect.

qa.q: How might the professor see students who return with progress?
qa.a: The professor likely feels the time was well spent and is more willing to help again, since the students show what the advice achieved.

grounding: After a meeting a student sends thanks with what was fixed and later returns with new work, turning a favour into an ongoing relationship.

subtype: Approach: trying another route when the first refuses [Revision]
passage:
Monday. Suraj went to the professor's office and asked whether the professor would guide the final-year project. "I am sorry," said the professor, "I am already handling six students and cannot give you proper time."

Tuesday. Suraj told Nilesh the news, disappointed, then said, "I should not stop there. I'll ask for a suggestion instead." Later that day Suraj sent a polite email: "Thank you for considering it. Could you suggest a colleague who works on soil sensors?"

Thursday. The professor replied with a name and a note of introduction. The new guide met Suraj and Nilesh the next week and liked the topic. Suraj wrote a thank-you back to the first professor.

qa.q: How many students was the professor already handling?
qa.a: The professor was already handling six students.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling after the first refusal, and what did Suraj decide?
qa.a: Suraj felt disappointed but decided not to stop there, and to ask politely for a suggestion instead.

qa.q: What could Suraj try if the colleague also has no space, and why?
qa.a: Suraj could ask the department for a list of guides working on similar topics, because the topic can match more than one person.

qa.q: How might the first professor see Suraj's follow-up email?
qa.a: The professor may feel respected and glad to help by naming a colleague, since the message was polite and did not press for a yes.

grounding: When a professor is too busy to guide a project, the student politely asks for a suggestion and is pointed to a suitable colleague.
